title: Quantitative study on the activation of the cellular immune system by flavor compounds in coffee
summary:
Food contains active compounds that not only stimulate our sense of taste and smell via specific receptors, but can also activate, via the same receptors, immune cells in the blood.
Previous studies have examined the uptake of caffeine and the activation of the immune system through receptors on blood cells. These studies found that the form of administration (coffee vs. pure caffeine) plays a significant role. This raised the question of whether other compounds in coffee might also influence the immune system. This study aims to investigate the effect of decaffeinated versus caffeinated coffee on the activation of the immune system via receptors on blood immune cells. In addition, a genetic analysis will be conducted to examine the activation of specific proteins and bitter taste receptors. A standardized taste test (the so-called PROP test) will also be used to assess individual sensitivity to bitter compounds. Furthermore, a coffee sensory analysis will be performed to determine the extent to which caffeine contributes to the bitterness of the coffee beverage.
conditions: Investigation of the immunological response in healthy adults following the consumption of decaffeinated coffee in comparison to caffeinated coffee.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
males and females
BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 kg/m2
aged between 18 and 40
Exclusion criteria:
Current tobacco consumption
Deviation from normal weight (BMI < 18.5 and > 24.9 kg/m2)
Practice of competitive sports (>10h/week)
Known metabolic disorders, lipid metabolism disorders, diabetes mellitus or untreated thyroid dysfunction
